fun_facts: Yellowfin tuna run warm-blooded in patches: a mesh of blood vessels called the rete mirabile lets them hold their swimming muscles, eyes and brain a few degrees above the surrounding water, sharpening vision and reaction time mid-strike -- modest compared to bluefin tuna, which can run over 20°C above ambient, but real all the same.

In the eastern Pacific, yellowfin tuna are famous for schooling directly beneath pods of spinner and spotted dolphins, closely enough that fishing fleets spent decades finding tuna by finding dolphins first; the same partnership is rare almost everywhere else the species turns up, including here in the Atlantic.

A yellowfin tuna can top 400 pounds and six feet in length, but it gets there fast and doesn't stick around: most live only six or seven years, so the biggest fish landed off the Carolinas are racing a clock as much as they're racing a hook.

measures.label: Fork length
measures.help: Measured along the curve of the body, from the tip of the upper jaw to the fork of the tail; curved fork length is the standard tuna measurement, and is what the federal minimum size is based on.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Yellowfin tuna cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: under the federal Atlantic HMS recreational minimum size for yellowfin tuna, 27 inches curved fork length
